summary: Defines a way to securely identify who sent a SIP message, which matters especially between domains. It adds an Identity header carrying a signature and an Identity-Info header pointing to the signer's certificate. It is a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 8224.

eli5.summary: A signature on a letter that proves who really wrote it, plus a note saying where to look up the signer. A newer note replaced it.

questions: what is the sip identity header
how does sip identity signing work
subtitle: A signed Identity header lets a domain vouch for who really sent a SIP request.

tldr.problem: The From header of a SIP request can be filled in with anything, so impersonation is easy, and the existing SIP security options (Digest, TLS, S/MIME) do not let a stranger check who sent a request.
tldr.mechanism: An authentication service in the sender's domain authenticates the sender, signs a hash of key header fields and the body with the domain's certificate, and adds an Identity header plus an Identity-Info header that points to the certificate.
tldr.outcome: A receiving domain can verify the signature and know the sender's domain authorized that From value. RFC 4474 was obsoleted by RFC 8224.

today: RFC 4474 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 8224, which is the specification to read for SIP identity today.

sections.title: Why SIP Needs Authenticated Identity
sections.content:
A SIP request names its sender in the From header field, but whoever controls a user agent can fill that field in arbitrarily. RFC 4474 notes that impersonation is therefore very simple, which defeats authorization policies such as a presence service checking subscribers against a whitelist, or a person reading a displayed Caller-ID.

The security tools in RFC 3261 do not solve this well. Few user agents have the end-user certificates needed for S/MIME, and Digest authentication needs a prearranged shared secret between originator and destination. Chained trust through mutual TLS between proxies is weaker than something checkable end to end. The P-Asserted-Identity approach only gives hop-by-hop trust inside a managed network of mutually trusting nodes.

This document instead defines an identity as a SIP URI, usually the address-of-record (AoR) such as sip:alice@atlanta.example.com, and lets the sender's own domain vouch for it. Its scope is SIP requests; responses are left for future work.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write any name on the outside of an envelope. This gives the sender's post office a way to prove the name on the envelope is real.

sections.title: Authentication Service and Verifier
sections.content:
The design adds two roles. An authentication service is a proxy server or user agent that holds the private key of a domain certificate. A proxy is the common choice because it usually has a stable hostname, a certificate and access to registrar capabilities for authenticating users. A verifier checks the result.

In the overview, Alice at example.com sends an INVITE over TLS to her domain's authentication service. It authenticates her, perhaps with a Digest challenge, and checks that she may use the identity in From. It then hashes selected headers and the body, signs the hash with the domain certificate and inserts an Identity header and a companion Identity-Info header. Bob's domain checks the signature, and so can Bob's user agent server.

The service must first confirm it is responsible for the domain in From; if not, it must not add an Identity header. It must add a Date header and a Content-Length header if missing, and it should reject a request whose Date differs from its own clock by more than ten minutes. Proxies must not remove or modify an existing Identity or Identity-Info header.
sections.eli5: Alice's post office checks that she is who she says she is, puts a seal on her letter, and leaves a note saying where to see what the seal looks like. Bob's post office checks the seal.

sections.title: The Identity and Identity-Info Headers
sections.content:
The signed value is built from a canonical string of fields joined by a vertical bar: the From addr-spec, the To addr-spec, the Call-ID, the CSeq number and method, the Date, the Contact addr-spec (empty if there is no Contact) and the message body. The result is signed with the algorithm named by the alg parameter of Identity-Info.

The only algorithm defined is rsa-sha1, which every implementation must support. It uses sha1WithRSAEncryption with a base64 result, and an RSA key of 1024 bits or longer must be used. Identity-Info carries a URI, which must dereference to the signer's certificate, plus a required alg parameter. Implementations must support HTTP and HTTPS URIs, and the resource has the form application/pkix-cert.

Each header can appear only once in a message. The mechanism does not protect CANCEL, and the headers must not appear in CANCEL. When a certificate is rolled over, services should give each new certificate a new URI and keep older ones available for longer than the plausible lifetime of a SIP message, for which an hour would most likely suffice.
sections.eli5: The seal is made from the important parts of the letter, such as who it is from, who it is for and when it was sent. If anyone changes those parts, the seal no longer matches.

sections.title: Verifier Behavior and Error Codes
sections.content:
A verifier works in order. It first gets the signing domain's certificate, ideally from a cache indexed by the Identity-Info URI, and validates it by the procedures of RFC 3280. It then checks that the signer is authoritative for the domain in From, rebuilds the canonical string and compares it with the signature, and finally validates the Date, Contact and Call-ID headers. The Date must fall in the certificate's validity period.

Four new SIP response codes report failures. If local policy requires an Identity header and none is present, the verifier sends 428. The other codes cover an unusable certificate URI, an untrusted certificate and a signature mismatch.

User agents need no change for the mechanism to work, but a user agent that can verify identities should show signed From values differently from unsigned ones. The sending UAC should protect its link to the authentication service, for example with TLS, because the mechanism gives no integrity between those two.
sections.eli5: The receiver looks up the seal, rebuilds it from the letter, and checks the two match. If they do not, it sends back a note saying what went wrong.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The signature covers more than From to stop replay and cut-and-paste attacks. The To header stops a valid Identity header being pasted into a request for another user. CSeq stops an INVITE being turned into a BYE. Verifiers must reject a stale Date (the recommended window is 3600 seconds) and must remember Call-IDs from valid requests for at least that long, so the Call-ID acts as a nonce.

The document is honest about limits. The headers cannot protect themselves, since an attacker can strip them. The display-name is not signed, because display-names are not unique. The Via header is not signed because an attacker could insert a further Via after it. An authentication service in an intermediary could still alter a message before signing, so users must trust their local domain. Domain certificates are checked by the procedures of RFC 2818 Section 3.1, and self-signed certificates should not be trusted without a prior key exchange.

For privacy, anonymous URIs with a valid domain can be signed, but anonymous.invalid cannot. Because Contact is signed, a privacy service cannot alter it after authentication without breaking the signature.
sections.eli5: The seal also covers the date and a one-of-a-kind ID, so a stolen seal cannot be used on a new letter or reused later. It cannot stop someone from tearing the seal off, though.

items.label: Use Identity Header
items.desc: Policy requires an Identity header and the request has none.

items.label: Bad Identity-Info
items.desc: The Identity-Info URI cannot be dereferenced.

items.label: Unsupported Certificate
items.desc: The verifier cannot validate the certificate.

items.label: Invalid Identity Header
items.desc: The signature does not match the digest-string the verifier computed.
